sections.title: Introduction and Evaluation of Earth Pressures
sections.summary: Apparent earth pressure (AEP) envelopes — not triangular active pressure — are used to design flexible anchored walls. For sands: trapezoidal, pa = 0.65 KA γH (Eq 10b); total load = 0.65 KA γH². For stiff-to-hard fissured clays: trapezoidal from Table 5 (ranges 0.2γH to 0.4γH maximum ordinate for permanent walls using drained parameters). For soft-to-medium clays: based on stability number Ns = γH/Su (Eq 9). For Ns ≤ 4, stiff clay envelope applies; for Ns > 5.14, modified soft clay envelope. AEP envelopes give conservative anchor loads for entire excavation history but do not predict actual loads at any stage.
sections.body:
Design steps for anchored walls (Table 4): (1) establish project requirements; (2) evaluate subsurface conditions; (3) evaluate design parameters and factors of safety; (4) establish wall and anchor geometry; (5) estimate earth pressures and water pressures; (6) calculate anchor loads; (7) design structural components; (8) evaluate overall stability; (9) evaluate wall and ground movements.

Apparent earth pressure envelopes: For flexible anchored walls constructed top-down, actual earth pressure distribution is not triangular active. Apparent earth pressure envelopes are trapezoidal empirical envelopes derived from field measurements. They provide conservative estimates of anchor loads and wall bending moments for the entire excavation history but do not represent actual load at any stage. Staged construction analyses (beam on elastic foundation) may be needed where actual loads are required.

Sand: Recommended trapezoidal AEP, pa = 0.65 KA γH (Eq 10b) over the middle 75% of wall height, with linear decrease to zero at top and bottom. Total load = 0.65 KA γH². Stability number not applicable.

Stiff to hard fissured clays: Trapezoidal envelopes from literature (Table 5 — Terzaghi and Peck 1967, Schnabel 1982, Winter 1990, Ulrich 1989, FHWA-RD-75-130 1976). For permanent walls, drained effective stress analysis is required because undrained strength may decrease over time in fissured OC clay. Use zero cohesion (fully softened) for permanent design.

Soft to medium clays: Stability number Ns = γH/Su (Eq 9) governs. For Ns > 5.14, the failure surface may penetrate significantly below the excavation base, requiring large lower anchor loads. Table 6 and limit equilibrium (Table 16, 17) methods used when Ns is large.

Water pressures: Permanent soldier beam and lagging walls typically designed with drainage. Net seepage pressure calculated from flownet; uniform surcharge: Δσh = K × qs (Eq 18).
key_points: AEP envelopes — trapezoidal, not triangular active — used for flexible anchored wall design
Sand: pa = 0.65 KA γH (Eq 10b) over middle 75% of wall; total load = 0.65 KA γH²
Stiff-hard clay: trapezoidal envelopes from Table 5; permanent walls require drained (zero cohesion) analysis
Soft-medium clay: stability number Ns = γH/Su governs; Ns > 5.14 → failure surface penetrates below excavation
AEP envelopes overestimate moments near subgrade and underestimate anchor loads vs. triangular assumption

sections.title: Ground Anchor Design
sections.summary: Anchor loads from the AEP diagram using the tributary area method. Total anchor load T resolved into horizontal (Th = T cosθ, Eq 20) and vertical (Tv = T sinθ, Eq 21) components. Minimum unbonded length: 4.5 m for strand, 3 m for bar; extend H/5 or 1.5 m behind critical failure surface. Maximum soil anchor bond length: 9–12 m (beyond that, capacity does not significantly increase). Rock anchor bond length: 3–10 m. Presumptive ultimate bond stresses from Table 7 (PTI 1996) for rock, cohesive, and cohesionless soils; pressure-grouted anchors achieve higher capacity than gravity-grouted. Anchor design load ≤ 60% SMTS; test load ≤ 80% SMTS. Anchor spacing ≥ 1.2 m horizontal and vertical.
sections.body:
Calculation of anchor loads: The tributary area method distributes the apparent earth pressure to each anchor level. For multi-level walls, each anchor carries the tributary area of the AEP diagram, and the reaction force R at the wall toe carries the bottom tributary area. Horizontal anchor load: Th = T cosθ (Eq 20); vertical anchor load: Tv = T sinθ (Eq 21).

Unbonded length: Minimum unbonded length is 4.5 m for strand tendons and 3 m for bar tendons, to prevent significant load reductions from anchor creep. Extend a minimum of H/5 or 1.5 m (whichever is greater) behind the critical potential failure surface to allow for minor load transfer in the grout column. The bond length must be located in appropriate ground for anchoring and at sufficient distance behind the failure surface.

Compression anchors: Designed so that the grout body is in compression rather than tension. May achieve higher capacity in certain soils. Two main types: Type 1 — tendon fixed at or near the bond zone bottom, so grout is compressed by a load plate; Type 2 — tendon fixed near the bond zone top, and the grout body transfers load to soil in compression.

Anchor bond length — soil: Maximum effective bond length is 9 to 12 m. Bond lengths greater than 12 m do not significantly increase capacity in uniform soil unless special procedures are used. Ultimate load transfer capacity estimated from soil type and SPT N (Table 6 for preliminary design). Presumptive ultimate bond stresses from Table 7 (PTI 1996): gravity-grouted cohesionless 0.07–0.14 MPa; pressure-grouted cohesionless higher; cohesive 0.03–0.07 MPa for gravity-grouted. Allowable anchor load = ultimate bond stress × π × D × L / FS (FS = 2.0 minimum).

Anchor bond length — rock: Typical bond lengths 3 to 10 m with minimum 3 m. Ultimate load from rock type (Table 8): granite/basalt 1.7–3.1 MPa; dolomitic limestone 1.4–2.1 MPa. Lower values if rock mass controlled by discontinuities.

Tendon selection: Design load ≤ 60% SMTS; temporary/test load ≤ 80% SMTS. Table 10: properties of 15-mm strands (ASTM A416 Grade 270). Performance tests load to 150% of design load. Proof tests load to 133% of design load.

Anchor spacing: Horizontal and vertical spacing ≥ 1.2 m. Uppermost anchor selected to minimize cantilever deformation and to ensure passive resistance is adequate during anchor proof testing.
key_points: Anchor load from tributary area of AEP diagram; Th = T cosθ (Eq 20), Tv = T sinθ (Eq 21)
Min unbonded length: 4.5 m (strand), 3 m (bar); extend H/5 or 1.5 m behind critical failure surface
Soil bond length: effective maximum 9–12 m; beyond 12 m, capacity does not increase significantly
Rock bond length: 3–10 m typical; ultimate bond from Table 8 (e.g., granite 1.7–3.1 MPa)
Table 7 (PTI 1996): presumptive ultimate bond stresses — cohesionless 0.07–0.14 MPa (gravity), cohesive 0.03–0.07 MPa

sections.title: Wall Structural Design and Embedded Portion Capacity
sections.summary: Soldier beam bending moments calculated by tributary area method. Allowable bending stress: Fb = 0.55 Fy for permanent/critical walls; 20% increase allowed for positive moments in temporary SOE walls. Steel: Grade 36 (Fy = 248 MPa) or Grade 50 (Fy = 345 MPa). Timber lagging thickness from Table 12. Lateral capacity of embedded wall from Broms method (for soldier beams) or Wang-Reese method; passive resistance reduced by FS = 1.5. Axial capacity: FS = 2.5 on skin friction and end bearing for clay; 2.0 on skin friction, 2.5 on end bearing for sand. β method: fs = β σ'v; β = 1.5 - 0.42z^0.34 for sands with N ≥ 15.
sections.body:
Wall bending moments: Calculated using the tributary area method (figures 38, 39). For competent soils, maximum bending moment occurs in the exposed portion of the wall. For walls penetrating deep weak deposits, the maximum may occur in the embedded portion. The bending moment from the tributary area method is multiplied by soldier beam spacing for soldier beams.

Allowable bending stress: Fb = 0.55 Fy for permanent walls and critical temporary walls. For temporary SOE walls, a 20% increase in allowable stress may be allowed for positive bending moments between anchors; no increase for negative moments at anchor locations or at toe. Steel grades: Grade 36 (Fy = 248 MPa) and Grade 50 (Fy = 345 MPa) most common.

Timber lagging: Thickness from Table 12 (after FHWA-RD-75-130, 1976) based on soil type, depth, and clear span between soldier beams (1.5–3.0 m). Table 12 covers competent soils, caving soils, and cohesive soils by USCS classification.

Lateral capacity of embedded portion: Anchored walls derive support from anchors and passive soil resistance below excavation subgrade. Prior to first anchor, wall acts as cantilever. Passive resistance evaluated by Broms method (for soldier beam and lagging walls) or Wang-Reese method. For sheet-pile walls, passive earth pressure coefficient reduced by FS = 1.5. Required embedment depth: passive resistance / reaction force R ≥ 1.5 (Broms); or per Wang-Reese. No passive resistance assumed over 1.5× soldier beam width above base (figure 41c).

Axial capacity of soldier beams: Driven or drilled-in per deep foundation methods (FHWA-HI-97-013). Interface friction = 0° assumed above excavation base. FS on skin friction and end bearing (Table 14): clay 2.5/2.5; sand 2.0/2.5. Effective stress analysis for driven beams in sand (β method): fs = β × po (Eq 25/29). For sands with N ≥ 15: β = 1.5 - 0.42z^0.34 (0.25 < β < 1.2). For N < 15: β = (N/15)(1.5 - 0.42z^0.34). For gravels: β = 2.0 - 0.15z^0.75. For drilled-in shafts in clay: unit end-bearing from Nc* factors (Table 15) and adhesion correlation (Figure 46 after Tomlinson 1980).
key_points: Allowable bending stress: Fb = 0.55 Fy (permanent); 20% increase allowed for SOE positive moments only

Lateral passive resistance FS = 1.5 for Broms and Wang-Reese; no passive over 1.5B above excavation base (soldier beams)
Axial FS: clay — 2.5 on friction, 2.5 on end bearing; sand — 2.0 on friction, 2.5 on end bearing

sections.title: Anchored Slopes, Landslide Stabilization, and Ground Mass Stability
sections.summary: Anchored slope stabilization uses ground anchors to increase the normal stress on the failure surface and provide a resisting force against sliding. Minimum design: one anchor level + wall penetrating failure surface, or two anchor levels. Anchor forces modeled in limit equilibrium as point loads at the wall-anchor intersection (components from horizontal and vertical). For deep soft clay, Ns = γH/Su governs basal stability: FS = Nc × Su / γH (Eq 37). External stability (overall rotational failure through anchor bond zone): FS ≥ 1.3.
sections.body:
Anchored slopes and landslide stabilization: Prestressed ground anchors act against the thrust of the potential slip surface and increase normal stress on it. A wall with one anchor level must penetrate the failure surface; a wall with two anchor levels need not penetrate the failure surface. The restraint force provided by ground anchors is modeled in limit equilibrium as a point load at the anchor-wall intersection; for Case 1 (wall penetrating failure surface), only horizontal component acts on the failure surface; for Case 2 (wall not penetrating), both horizontal and vertical components act.

Basal stability (soft to medium clay): Bottom heave potential evaluated using Terzaghi bearing capacity approach. For excavations with wide footprint where shearing resistance along exterior of failure block is negligible:
FS = Nc × Su / γH (Eq 37)
For shallow deposits or narrow excavations:
FS = Nc × Su / γH + Ds × Su / (γH × B) (Eq 36)
where Nc is from Figure 51 (depends on H/B and B/L), Ds is depth to hard stratum below excavation. Minimum FS for basal stability depends on site conditions.

External stability (overall rotation through anchor bond zone): Modeled as slope stability problem. Critical failure surfaces include deep circular failure through and behind the wall. FS ≥ 1.3 minimum; FS ≥ 1.5 for critical permanent applications.
key_points: Minimum anchored slope design: one anchor + wall penetrating failure surface, or two anchors + wall above failure surface
Limit equilibrium model: anchor force as point load at wall-anchor intersection
Basal stability: FS = Nc × Su / γH for wide excavation in soft clay (Eq 37)
External stability: FS ≥ 1.3 (minimum); FS ≥ 1.5 for critical permanent applications

sections.title: Tiedown Design, Seismic Design, and Other Issues
sections.summary: Tiedown anchor design resists hydrostatic or overturning uplift. Rock tiedowns: bond zone in compression at 45° cone; FS = 2–3 against rock mass failure. Soil tiedowns: uplift capacity Qu = Qtu + Qsu (Eq 38). Seismic design: Mononobe-Okabe equation with horizontal seismic coefficient kh and vertical coefficient kv; AASHTO uses kh = 0.5A (A = PGA from seismic risk map, 10% in 50 years); permanent seismic deformations from Hynes and Franklin (1984) chart. Wall movements ≤ 0.1% to 0.5% of wall height. Drainage systems behind anchored walls to prevent hydrostatic pressure buildup.
sections.body:
Tiedown design: Tiedowns resist vertical uplift from hydrostatic or overturning forces. Rock tiedowns resist uplift via a rock cone failure at ~45° from anchorage; FS = 2 to 3 against overall rock mass stability per BS8081 (1989). The conservative 45° cone assumption means actual FS is typically higher. Soil tiedowns: Uplift capacity Qu = Qtu + Qsu (Eq 38) where Qtu = tip resistance (typically small, often neglected) and Qsu = side resistance from ground-grout bond. For hydrostatic tiedowns (e.g., Boston Central Artery), critical issues include watertight connections and load variations from groundwater level changes.

Seismic design: Pseudo-static analysis using Mononobe-Okabe (M-O) equation. Seismic active earth pressure coefficient KAE from Figure 56. AASHTO (1996) seismic coefficient kh = 0.5A (A = PGA, 10% probability of exceedance in 50 years). Vertical coefficient kv = 0 to 0.2A. For potentially liquefiable soils, densification or other ground improvement methods should be applied. Permanent seismic deformations estimated using Hynes and Franklin (1984) chart (Figure 58).

Wall and ground movements: Horizontal movements at top of wall typically 0.1% to 0.5% of wall height; vertical settlements behind wall 0 to 0.5% of wall height extending to about 3H behind the wall. Maximum wall movement typically at mid-height. Several sources of movement: cantilever (first anchor), wall settlement (end bearing mobilization), elastic elongation of tendon, anchor yielding/load redistribution.

Drainage: Horizontal drains installed at back of wall; prefabricated drainage composites. Anchored walls interfere with natural drainage in existing slopes — hydrostatic buildup must be relieved.
key_points: Rock tiedown FS = 2–3 against 45° cone failure (BS8081); conservative assumption means actual FS higher
Soil tiedown uplift: Qu = Qtu + Qsu; side resistance governs for deep anchors
Seismic: AASHTO kh = 0.5A (A = PGA from risk map, 10%/50yr); Mononobe-Okabe for KAE
Horizontal wall movement typically 0.1–0.5% of wall height; vertical settlement extends to ~3H behind wall
Drainage systems required behind anchored walls — hydrostatic pressure buildup is a common failure cause
